# dsh-thinking-effort
**English** | 简体中文

Bring back the **thinking-intensity picker** (推理等级 / reasoning effort) for third-party API keys in
D

*thinking-intensity picker** (推理等级 / reasoning effort) for third-party API keys in
DeepSeek Harness.

You plug an OpenAI-compatible relay into `dsh`, pick one of its models, and the
「推理等级」 pane in the c

omposer is simply gone. This plugin declares the missing capability for
those routes, so the picker

comes back — from a slash command, from the Plugins page, or by asking
the model.
## What this plugin does

It writes that declaration — in the one place the adapter reads it, through the supported settings
s

eam. No adapter takeover, no HTTP interception, no harness patch. By default it does so
**automatica

lly at startup**: any third-party route with no declaration is filled in, so installing
the plugin i

any third-party route with no declaration is filled in, so installing
the plugin is the whole setup.
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Four entry points over one shared, unit-tested planner:
| Surface | How |
| Automatic | **Nothing to run**: a load-time pass declares every third-party route that has none |
| Slash command | `/thinking` · `/thinking presets` · `/thinking adapt` · `/thinking set <provider>/

<model> <preset>` · `/thinking remove …` |
| Plugins page | Sidebar **Plugins** → **dsh-thinking-eff

ort** → per-model dropdown, applies instantly |
| Model tool | `thinking_effort_status` / `thinking_
effort_set`, so "这个模型调不了思考强度" gets fixed conversationally |
A load-time diagnostic also names every route that still cannot be adjusted, so a freshly added key
is noticed immediately instead of the first time you open the model picker.
### Compatibility

Built for dsh **0.2.2-rc.1**. The peer dependencies pin that release, `engines.dsh` declares
`>=0.2.
1-rc.2 <0.3.0`, and `dsh.manifestVersion` records the 0.2.1 package-manifest format.
The integration points are the 0.2.2 ones: host writes go through `ctx.settings.mutate` (path ops),

the browser card through the settings domain's `ctx.configForms` service, and a third-party
bundle's

own configuration page registers in the `plugins.bundle.config` slot of the sidebar
**Plugins** pag

e. The pre-0.2 client binder (`settingsScope`) no longer exists in dsh, so versions
before 0.2.1 are

client binder (`settingsScope`) no longer exists in dsh, so versions
before 0.2.1 are not supported.
### What automatic adaptation decides

It only touches **configuration-declared** routes — a catalog route already resolves its models'
cap

ability from the installed catalog, so a declaration there would only narrow it. For each route it
r
eads the evidence already in the configuration:
1. If pi-ai already believes the endpoint does **not** take `reasoning_effort` (xAI, Z.AI, Moonshot,

Together, NVIDIA, Cloudflare, or your own `compat.supportsReasoningEffort: false`), it writes
`open

ai-null-off`. Sending `xhigh` to an endpoint that does not parse the parameter is the one way
this p

lugin could turn a missing picker into a failing request. Your explicit setting outranks the
plugin'

s inference.
2. Otherwise, if the endpoint host identifies a vendor (`deepseek.com`, `openrouter.ai`

, DashScope,
…), it writes that vendor's preset.
3. Otherwise it writes `autoAdaptPreset`, `passthro

ugh` by default: all seven levels sent under their
own names, no dialect pinned. A gateway with its
own ladder gets the whole ladder back that way.
It never overwrites a model you already declared, and never touches `reasoningEfforts: false` — that
is an explicit "this model does not reason", and adaptation must not undo it.

Adaptation supplies the *declaration*; it cannot verify that the endpoint honours these values,
beca

use that is not discoverable from configuration. After seeing the log line, check what each level
ac
tually sends with `/thinking explain`, then try a level in a session.
## How it works

Writes are **path-addressed settings mutations**:
`settings.mutate(entryId, settingsOps(provider, pa

tch), revision)`. Each op names one path —
`providers.<route>.models`, `providers.<route>.modelOverr

ides.<model>`,
`providers.<route>.reasoning` — so only the edited route (and, inside a catalog route

, only the
edited model) is touched; sibling routes and unowned fields survive without a read-modify

-write.
The browser card sends the same op list through `ctx.configForms`, so the command, the tools

and
the GUI cannot write different documents.

The shape of the patch depends on where the route's capability comes from, because `llm-pi-ai`
refus
es `modelOverrides` on a route that also carries a `models` list:

- a route with a non-empty `models` list (every hand-declared third-party route) → the list is
**rew

ritten in full**, carrying every entry and every unowned field through;
- a route inheriting the ins

talled catalog → one `modelOverrides.<model>` entry, set as its own
path op so the rest of the dict

→ one `modelOverrides.<model>` entry, set as its own
path op so the rest of the dict keeps serving.
One side effect is worth knowing before you read the diff. The rewritten `models` array is built fro

m
the *resolved* section, so schema defaults the resolver had already materialized ride along into t

he
stored document — after declaring a level on a hand-declared route, that model entry typically ga

ins
`compat.chatTemplateKwargs: {}` and `compat.chatTemplateArgs: {}` beside the `thinkingFormat` th

is
plugin actually wrote. They are the schema's own defaults, so the resolved value is unchanged and

nothing behaves differently; the document just becomes explicit about fields it previously left
imp

licit. The write stays narrow at the route level: only the route you named appears in the user
layer
, and no route-level default is materialized.

Writes are revision-fenced against the descriptor read in the same pass (a concurrent editor is
repo

rted, then retried once against a fresh read), and a declaration that is already in force writes
